summary: Directs IANA on which RPKI objects it should issue. This gives the number-resource hierarchy a defined handling for reserved and unallocated resources, so none can be falsely authorized.

eli5.summary: This is a to-do list for the organization that keeps internet records, telling it what digital papers to sign for resources nobody has been given.

questions: what rpki objects does iana issue
why does iana issue roas for reserved address space
subtitle: Tells IANA which RPKI objects to sign, and which to leave unsigned, for the address and AS number space nobody is meant to route.

tldr.problem: IANA manages reserved, unallocated and special-purpose IPv4, IPv6 and AS number resources for the IETF, and RFC 6480 directs it to issue RPKI objects for them, but the choice of which objects to issue was not spelled out.
tldr.mechanism: IANA sets up an RPKI CA covering these resources and issues AS 0 ROAs for resources not intended to be routed, no ROAs at all for those meant to be routed, plus a ghostbusters record, a manifest and a CRL.
tldr.outcome: Resources that should never appear in global routing get a signed statement saying so, while resources that are meant to be routed are left alone. This is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

facts.label: Multicast AS 0 ROAs
facts.value: MUST be issued for listed ranges

today: RFC 6491 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The document says it will be revised if IANA is directed to issue additional RPKI objects.

sections.title: What IANA Is Asked to Issue
sections.content:
"An Infrastructure to Support Secure Internet Routing" (RFC 6480) directs IANA to issue Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) objects for which it is authoritative. This document describes those objects.

The objects cover the unallocated, reserved and special use IPv4 and IPv6 address blocks, and the unallocated and reserved Autonomous System numbers. IANA manages these number resources for the IETF, so IANA is responsible for issuing the matching RPKI objects. If IANA is later directed to issue more kinds of object, this document is to be revised.

The document does not deal with BGP routing systems, which are under the policy control of the organizations that run them. Operators who want to use unallocated, reserved or special use space locally are pointed to a work-in-progress document on local trust anchor management.
sections.eli5: The keeper of the internet's number lists is told which official papers to sign for numbers that nobody has been given.

sections.title: Key Terms and the AS 0 ROA
sections.content:
A Route Origination Authorization (ROA) lets the holder of an address prefix say which AS may originate routes for it in BGP. An AS 0 ROA is a ROA with the value 0 in the ASID field. Per RFC 6483, it is an attestation by the prefix holder that the prefix, and any more specific prefix, should not be used in a routing context.

The RFC also defines the phrase "Not intended to be (publicly) routed": prefixes that are not meant to be in the global Internet routing table, for example 192.168/16.

The RFC notes that the addresses it lists are not example addresses, so they do not follow the documentation-address RFCs. This is intentional, because the text is about specific real addresses.
sections.eli5: An AS 0 ROA is a sign that says nobody is allowed to use this address. It is how you mark land as off limits.

sections.title: Reserved, Unallocated and Special Purpose Resources
sections.content:
For reserved IPv4 and IPv6 resources held back by IETF action, such as 127.0.0.0/8, IANA SHOULD issue an AS 0 ROA when the resource is not intended to be routed. A small number of reserved resources are intended to be routed, for example 192.88.99.0/24, and for those IANA MUST NOT issue any ROAs, AS 0 or otherwise.

For unallocated resources, meaning those not yet allocated for special purposes, to Regional Internet Registries or to others, the RFC treats them as not intended to be globally routed. IANA SHOULD issue an AS 0 ROA for all of them.

For special purpose registry resources, it depends on the routing intent. 2001::/32 is an example intended for global routing, and 2001:002::/48 is an example that is not. IANA MUST NOT issue ROAs for the first kind and SHOULD issue an AS 0 ROA for the second.

The RFC says SHOULD, not MUST, on purpose. An AS 0 ROA may be removed or not yet issued before an IANA registry action, and IANA should not be put in a position where its normal internal operations contradict IETF standards.
sections.eli5: If a plot is empty or off limits, put up a do-not-use sign. If a plot is meant to be used, put up no sign at all.

sections.title: Multicast Ranges
sections.content:
Some registrations in the IPv4 and IPv6 multicast registries are not intended to be globally routed. For these, IANA MUST issue an AS 0 ROA.

The IPv4 ranges listed are the Local Network Control Block (224.0.0.0 to 224.0.0.255), the IANA reserved portions of RESERVED (224.1.0.0 to 224.1.255.255), and the RESERVED ranges 224.5.0.0 to 224.251.255.255 and 225.0.0.0 to 231.255.255.255. For IPv6 the list is the node-local scope and link-local scope multicast addresses.

IANA MUST NOT issue any ROAs for any other multicast addresses unless directed by an IESG-approved Standards Track document with an appropriate IANA Considerations section.
sections.eli5: A few of the shout-to-everyone address ranges only work inside one room or one hallway. Those get the do-not-use sign for the wider world.

sections.title: Ghostbusters Record, CA, Manifests and CRLs
sections.content:
IANA MUST issue a ghostbusters object (RFC 6493) with content appropriate for the resources it maintains. This is an informational object at a publication point of an RPKI repository.

Before IANA can issue a ROA, it MUST first establish an RPKI Certification Authority that covers unallocated, reserved and special use number resources. The CA certificate MUST carry the RFC 3779 extensions for those resources, and the CA MUST issue a single-use end-entity (EE) certificate for each ROA it generates. EE certificates follow the Resource Certificate Profile (RFC 6487) and the constraints in RFC 6482.

IANA MUST maintain a publication point for this CA, MUST publish manifests (RFC 6486) there, and MUST issue a CRL under the CA certificate for the EE certificates. All objects follow the RPKI Certificate Policy (RFC 6484).
sections.eli5: Before signing anything, the keeper needs an official stamp, a one-time pass for every sign, a list of what has been posted and a list of cancelled passes.

sections.title: IANA and Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document directs IANA to issue, or refrain from issuing, the specific RPKI objects described for the current set of reserved, unallocated and special registry Internet Number Resources. IANA MUST also notify all other INR registries that it has issued RPKI objects for these resources, to avoid duplicate objects that might confuse relying parties.

The security section is brief. The document does not alter the security profile of the RPKI from that already discussed in SIDR working group documents.

Two appendices list the IANA reserved IPv4 and IPv6 blocks with the RFC behind each reservation and a To Be Routed flag. They were correct at the time of writing. Only 192.88.99.0/24 is marked Yes for IPv4, 192.0.0.0/24 is marked Various, and the rest are marked No.
sections.eli5: The keeper must tell the other record keepers what it signed so nobody signs the same thing twice and causes confusion.
